newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS- UK utilities weather in-line windfall tax.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS- UK utilities weather in-line windfall tax.

text.p: Britain's Labour government said on Wednesday it would raise 5.2 billion pounds ($8.6 billion) through a tax on privatised utilities, much as expected, and analysts said despite grumblings, companies should be able to weather the take.

"It's much in line, it's one-off which is good news, payment over two years is also helpful...I don't suppose there's going to be too much lack of sleep tonight," said Marshall Whiting, an analyst with SGST.

Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown told parliament that the levy would raise around 2.1 billion pounds from the electricity sector, some 1.65 billion from water companies and 1.45 billion from others.
The tax will be based on the difference between the value of companies at privatisation and a calculation related to net profits up to the first four years after sell-off.
It will be paid in two instalments, the first on December 1, 1997 and the second a year later.
The levy will cover water and electricity companies, airport operator BAA, former British Gas companies BG Plc and Centrica, British Telecommunications (BT) and Railtrack.
Several companies criticised the tax, which BT chairman Sir Iain Vallance described as a "tax on success not on excess."
Yorkshire Water, itself slammed for poor handling of a severe drought in 1995, said the tax was unwelcome, adding that it was "retrospective taxation which is bad news for investors."

Anglian Water threatened that borrowing to pay for the tax could hit funding special projects, such as improvements to water supplies in drought-stricken areas and possible future price reductions, while BG described the tax as "a blow".

U.S.-owned Midlands Electricity, Anglian Water, Railtrack and BAA all said they would have to borrow to fund the tax, which is aimed at the "excess profits" the government claims were made by utilities, privatised by previous Conservative administrations.
Railtrack said its share of the levy was likely to be up to 160 million pounds while BAA put its tax hit at 70 to 100 million and Southern Electric estimated it would pay around 165 million.
Anglian Water said it expected to pay 170 million and Midlands said it would pay 130 million.
Centrica could face a bill for 150-200 million, industry sources said, while BT said it expected to pay some 500 million pounds, below earlier speculation of around one billion.
Analysts said markets should be relieved that the total tax was near expectations and that it was simple to calculate which should give certainty.
"It's not as bad as it might have been...(Brown) has gone for a basis which is designed to give certainty...which I think the markets should welcome," said Richard Savours of Coopers & Lybrand.

The tax, which will fund a 3.5 billion pound programme aimed at cutting youth unemployment, was part of Labour's manifesto and proved highly popular with voters, helping to bring it to power with a landslide victory in the May 1 election.
Privatised utilities had become deeply unpopular, criticised for high dividend payouts, hefty executive pay packets and poor service.
Several companies have said they might consider a legal challenge to the tax, but analysts said its broad base might make this difficult.
BT and BAA said before the budget that they could consider a legal challenge, but the government has described the legislation as "watertight".
A BT spokesman said on Wednesday that the company would consider how to proceed once the finance bill had been published.
But he added that Brown appeared "to have taken account of the special characteristics of BT in determining the formula for devising the tax", which could help the board decide on its next move.
